content:
The first riot began with a broken window.

That was what everyone said afterward.

It was not true.

It began months earlier with wages that favored benders for work machines could not yet do. With landlords charging nonbender families more because they were considered less useful in emergency repairs. With factory owners hiring earthbenders to replace whole crews, then blaming the workers for being angry. With politicians promising fairness while quietly accepting money from people who profited from resentment.

The window was only the moment anger learned where to throw itself.

I was in the western district when glass shattered.

A nonbender workers’ meeting had filled the assembly hall. Most people were there to demand representation on the new municipal labor board. Outside, a smaller group of bending workers had gathered after rumors spread that the meeting wanted to ban bending in factories.

The rumor was false.

That did not make it powerless.

Someone threw a bottle.

Someone else threw stone.

Then the street split into sides.

I climbed onto a cart and shouted until my throat hurt.

“Nobody is banning bending!”

A man yelled back, “Tell them that!”

“I am them!”

That confused him for half a second.

It was not enough.

A slab of earth rose from the street.

Before it could fly, another wall of stone punched up in front of it.

Toph stood in the intersection.

“Anybody who bends another rock,” she shouted, “gets to explain it to me.”

The street went still.

Toph had that effect.

Katara arrived from the opposite side with clinic volunteers. Water curled around her arms, not as a weapon but as a visible warning.

Aang came down from the sky.

The crowd changed the instant they saw him.

Some people cheered.

Others booed.

That was new.

Aang heard both.

I saw it land.

He did not let it change his face.

“Everyone back,” he called. “No one here is your enemy.”

A voice from the crowd answered, “Easy for a bender to say!”

Another shouted, “He’s the Avatar! He protects everybody!”

“Then why are nonbenders still begging for seats on the board?”

The argument surged again.

Aang raised both hands.

Wind spread through the street in a broad pulse—not enough to knock anyone down, only enough to force space between bodies.

People stumbled backward.

The anger sharpened.

I knew immediately it had been a mistake.

So did Aang.

A woman near the front pointed at him. “See? When we get loud, the Avatar pushes us back.”

“That wasn’t—” Aang began.

I grabbed his sleeve.

“Stop.”

His eyes flashed toward me.

“Let them talk.”

“They’re going to hurt each other.”

“Toph has the street. Katara has the injured. Let them talk.”

Aang’s jaw tightened.

For a second I felt the full distance between us.

Not lover and lover.

Avatar and clerk.

Power and the person asking it to wait.

Then he lowered his hands.

The wind died.

I stepped onto the cart again.

“If you came for the labor board meeting, stay on this side. If you came because somebody told you we want to ban bending, you were lied to.”

Shouting.

I kept going.

“The proposal is on the wall inside. Read it. It asks for equal representation from bending and nonbending workers. Equal. Not removal.”

A man with a burn scar across one cheek shouted, “Then why did my brother lose his job to three earthbenders?”

“Because the factory owner could pay three people less than twelve.”

That answer changed the direction of several faces.

I pointed toward the mill at the end of the street.

“Your problem is not the earthbender standing next to you. Your problem is the man paying both of you as little as he can get away with.”

Toph made an approving noise.

Someone laughed.

The crowd did not calm all at once.

Nothing real happened all at once.

But questions replaced some of the shouting.

The meeting moved outside because the hall windows were broken. Bending workers who had come to protest stayed to listen. Katara passed bandages and tea. Toph leaned against a wall like a threat available on request.

Aang stayed behind me.

He did not speak again until someone asked him directly.

“What will the Avatar do?”

Aang looked at me first.

Not for permission.

For perspective.

Then he answered.

“I’ll support a board where neither benders nor nonbenders can make rules for the other without them in the room.”

A woman asked, “Will you sit on it?”

“No.”

That surprised everyone.

Aang continued, “If I take the deciding seat every time people disagree, nobody learns how to share power without me.”

The answer was not perfect.

It was better.

By nightfall the street had emptied.

Broken glass remained beneath the windows.

I helped sweep it.

Aang picked up a broom beside me.

For several minutes we worked without talking.

Finally he said, “You were angry at me.”

“Yes.”

“For using airbending.”

“For deciding that because you could control the crowd physically, you should.”

He stopped sweeping.

“I was trying to stop a fight.”

“I know.”

“Someone could have been killed.”

“I know.”

The frustration in his face rose.

“Then what was I supposed to do?”

There was no easy answer.

That mattered too.

“I don’t know,” I said.

Aang blinked.

“I know what you did felt wrong from where I stood. I know the nonbenders who were already afraid of being controlled saw the Avatar move their bodies without asking. I also know if you had done nothing and someone died, I’d be furious.”

His shoulders lowered a fraction.

“So I failed either way.”

“No.”

I set the broom against the wall.

“You faced a problem without a clean answer. That’s not the same thing as failure.”

Aang looked exhausted.

I took his hand.

“Listen to the part that hurt people. Keep the part that prevented injury. Figure out what you do differently next time.”

He squeezed my fingers.

“That sounds like something Katara would say.”

“She’s a bad influence.”

Toph’s voice came from the doorway. “Excuse me?”

Katara stood beside her carrying four cups of tea.

“You were listening?” I asked.

Toph shrugged. “The ground was.”

Katara handed Aang a cup.

He looked at her. “Was I wrong?”

Katara did not answer quickly.

“I think you were scared.”

“That’s not the same question.”

“No,” she said. “It’s the reason I’m not going to answer with a simple yes or no.”

Toph took her tea. “I would’ve dropped everybody into waist-deep holes.”

Three of us stared at her.

“What? They can’t riot if they can’t move.”

Aang started laughing.

Katara tried not to.

I failed immediately.

Toph looked pleased with herself.

The laughter did not erase the fault line running through the city.

It reminded us we were still standing on it together.

That night I wrote three pages of recommendations for the labor board.

Aang added notes in the margins.

Katara corrected my medical staffing estimate.

Toph drew a rock crushing a bag of money beside the section on factory owners.

I left it in the final draft.

The day after the riot, we walked the eastern district together without uniforms, titles, or guards.

That had been Katara’s idea.

“If we only come here when something is on fire,” she said, “people will learn that destruction is the fastest way to be seen.”

So we listened.

A nonbender machinist showed Toph how a poorly placed loading platform forced workers into the path of moving carts. Toph crouched, pressed two fingers to the stone, and asked three questions so technical I lost the thread.

A firebender who owned a bakery told Aang his oven permits had been delayed because officials assumed any industrial flame required extra inspection.

“That makes no sense,” Aang said.

“It makes paperwork,” I replied.

Katara spent nearly an hour with two mothers who wanted a permanent clinic but disagreed violently about where it should go.

Nobody solved the city that day.

That mattered.

We were not collecting suffering so we could perform wisdom at it. We were learning where the pressure lived before the next window broke.

On the walk home, Aang looked exhausted.

“Peace is easier when there are only two armies,” he said.

Toph snorted. “No, it isn’t.”

“You know what I mean.”

“I do. Still wrong.”

Katara slipped her hand into his.

I walked on his other side.

The city beneath us remained cracked in places. Fault lines did not vanish because we had finally learned their names.

The final draft was ugly, specific, and impossible to summarize into a slogan. That made me trust it more. Real repair usually looked less dramatic than the breaking: inspection schedules, translated notices, safer routes, people assigned to call back when someone complained.

Toph’s rock crushing the moneybag remained the clearest graphic in the packet.

A week later, one of those inspection schedules prevented another overloaded platform from collapsing. Nobody called that heroic. I thought about it all day.

Quiet prevention became its own kind of victory.
